lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Ask what killed five million four hundred thousand people in Congo between nineteen ninety eight and two thousand seven, and the answer people reach for is a battlefield.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The International Rescue Committee's own mortality surveys found fewer than one in ten of those deaths came from violence at all. The rest came from malaria, diarrhea, and hunger, in a country whose clinics and roads had stopped functioning.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The deadliest conflict since the Second World War did not start with an army crossing a border to conquer territory. It started with an army crossing a border to chase its own refugees.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Congo Wars. Nineteen ninety six to two thousand three.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On October eighteenth, nineteen ninety six, a rebel alliance calling itself the AFDL crosses from Rwanda into eastern Zaire.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Laurent-Desire Kabila leads it, a rebel who has been fighting since the nineteen sixties, once dismissed by Che Guevara as lacking revolutionary seriousness.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Behind him stand the Rwandan Patriotic Army under Paul Kagame, the Ugandan People's Defence Force under Yoweri Museveni, and the Angolan army.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Their stated target is the Interahamwe genocidaires who fled Rwanda two years earlier and reconstituted in the refugee camps across this same border.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Mobutu Sese Seko, who has ruled Zaire for thirty two years, sends his own army to stop them. His soldiers loot Kisangani instead of defending it.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Kabila enters Kinshasa on May the seventeenth, nineteen ninety seven. Mobutu flees to Morocco. The country is renamed the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A war that starts as a hunt for other people's killers ends, fourteen months later, with the hunter turning on the men who financed the hunt.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Kabila expels his Rwandan military advisors from Kinshasa in July nineteen ninety eight.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On August the second, Rwanda and Uganda back a new rebellion, the RCD, and invade eastern Congo a second time.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Kabila calls for help. Zimbabwe sends eleven thousand troops. Angola sends its air force. Namibia, Chad, and Sudan contribute forces of their own.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: By early nineteen ninety nine, nine African nations have soldiers on Congolese soil.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The International Rescue Committee's own report puts a name to what nine armies on one country's soil had become.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: The conflict in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has been aptly called Africa's first world war, involving at least seven foreign armies and affecting populations across an area the size of Western Europe.

segments.author: International Rescue Committee
segments.work: Mortality in the Democratic Republic of Congo: An Ongoing Crisis

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Lusaka Ceasefire Agreement, signed in July nineteen ninety nine, is violated before the ink dries.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Laurent-Desire Kabila is shot by his own bodyguard, Rashidi Kasereka, in the marble salon of the Palais de la Nation. He is sixty one.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: His son, Joseph Kabila, a twenty nine year old major general, is installed as president within ten days.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Joseph Kabila reopens peace negotiations. The Inter-Congolese Dialogue, brokered in Sun City, South Africa, produces a power sharing agreement in December two thousand two.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Foreign armies formally withdraw. The war is declared over on July the first, two thousand three.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Eastern Congo never receives that message.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The United Nations mission, MONUC, has grown to twenty thousand troops, the largest peacekeeping deployment in the world, at a cost exceeding one point three billion dollars a year.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On the night of November the fourth, forces of the CNDP under Laurent Nkunda enter the town of Kiwanja and kill an estimated one hundred fifty civilians.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The MONUC base is three kilometers away. Survivors who run toward it expecting protection receive none.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A joint investigation by Human Rights Watch and the United Nations documents house to house executions and bodies left in the street.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Denis Mukwege opens Panzi Hospital in Bukavu on September the fifteenth, nineteen ninety nine, expecting to deliver babies.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Within three months, the women arriving have injuries no obstetric training prepared him for: gang rape, and deliberate vaginal destruction designed to cause fistula.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: By two thousand eighteen, Panzi has treated over fifty thousand survivors. Armed men had already come to his home in Bukavu in October two thousand twelve and killed his guard at the gate. Mukwege survived because a neighbor's car happened to arrive.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In two thousand eighteen he accepts the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo alongside Nadia Murad.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Denis Mukwege tells the room in Oslo what fifty thousand patients had already told him.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: My body, and the bodies of all women in the eastern Congo, had been turned into a battlefield. The world has remained silent, unmoved, while we are crying.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A war declared over in two thousand three does not end for a surgeon still operating on it fifteen years later.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Five accounts of a war fought by seven armies, that killed by disease more than by bullets, and that has never entirely stopped.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The case starts with a number. Between July and November nineteen ninety four, roughly one point seven million Hutu refugees crossed from Rwanda into eastern Zaire.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Among them were an estimated thirty thousand to forty thousand former Rwandan soldiers and Interahamwe militiamen, the men who had just killed eight hundred thousand Tutsis in one hundred days. They retrained in the camps and raided back across the border.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A Canadian general, Maurice Baril, proposed a multinational force to disarm the camps. No country volunteered troops.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Rwanda's government, led by Paul Kagame, framed the nineteen ninety six intervention as the pursuit of genocidaires the world had refused to disarm. The journalist Philip Gourevitch, who worked in these camps, found the logic hard to dismiss.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: The men in those camps had just finished killing 800,000 people. They were training to do it again. And the world's response was to feed them.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: From this side, the word war is a euphemism. What happened was an invasion disguised as liberation, sustained by an extraction economy disguised as free trade.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: When Kabila tried to govern independently, expelling his Rwandan advisors, Rwanda and Uganda backed a new rebellion against him within weeks. Its leaders held titles, not power. It was commanded from Kigali.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Uganda controlled Ituri and Orientale Province for gold, timber, and diamonds. Rwanda controlled North and South Kivu for coltan, cassiterite, and wolframite. The United Nations Panel of Experts named eighty five companies profiting from what came out of the ground.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Congolese army, the FARDC, offered no protection. It went months without pay, and it committed mass rape of its own in Fizi and Minova. One Congolese civil society leader, unnamed in the record, quoted in Jason Stearns' account of the war, put it plainly.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: Everyone came to Congo to eat. Rwanda ate the east. Uganda ate the north. Zimbabwe ate the mines. And the Congolese ate nothing.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In two thousand, the price of coltan rose from fifty dollars a kilogram to four hundred. The cause was the mobile phone: every handset needed a tantalum capacitor, and eastern Congo holds sixty to eighty percent of the world's known reserves.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The United Nations Panel of Experts traced the supply chain from artisanal mines at Bisie, Walikale, and Rubaya through trading houses in Goma and Bukavu to smelters in Rwanda, Uganda, Malaysia, and China. By the time the tantalum reached a circuit board in Shenzhen, its origin was untraceable.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Dodd-Frank Act's conflict minerals provision, signed in two thousand ten, was the first legislative answer. Compliance cost an estimated three to four billion dollars in its first year, and the rule was later weakened.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The political scientist Severine Autesserre, who spent years in fieldwork across the Kivus, warned that the resource story comforted people because it implied a fix: regulate the supply chain and the killing stops. It did not stop.

lines.speaker: F
lines.text: The international focus on conflict minerals has created a convenient fiction, that eastern Congo's violence is about greed, not governance. It is about both.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The United Nations mission was established in November nineteen ninety nine with a mandate to monitor a ceasefire. Monitor. Not enforce. Not protect. That distinction defined everything after it.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: By two thousand ten it had grown to twenty thousand troops at one point three billion dollars a year, the largest and most expensive peacekeeping operation in United Nations history, spread across a territory the size of Western Europe with almost no roads.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Troop contributing countries kept national command over their own soldiers, so orders from the field competed with orders from home capitals. Some contingents protected civilians well. Others would not leave their base after dark.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A MONUC peacekeeper, unnamed in the record, was quoted afterward by Human Rights Watch about the night at Kiwanja.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: We knew what was happening in Kiwanja. We could hear the gunshots from our base. We did not have authorization to move.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Every armed group in eastern Congo used rape as a weapon: the FDLR, the CNDP, the Mai-Mai, the Rwandan and Ugandan armies, and the FARDC, Congo's own government army.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A two thousand eleven study estimated eleven hundred fifty two women were raped every day across the country, forty eight an hour. Even researchers who challenged the sample size agreed on the direction: the true number is in the hundreds of thousands.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Denis Mukwege developed reconstructive surgical techniques that did not exist in any textbook, because the injuries had not existed before Panzi Hospital opened.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In Oslo, having named the armed groups, the governments, and the corporations buying the minerals, Mukwege ended with a request rather than a demand.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: If you choose not to intervene, do not disturb. Please, have the decency to not look the other way.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: What each of these accounts does not carry.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Rwandan case leaves out its own soldiers' killing of unarmed Hutu civilians during the advance: six hundred seventeen incidents that the United Nations Mapping Report later described in language that could constitute genocide, a finding Kagame called immoral, and Rwanda's continued profit from the minerals it said it only wanted to secure.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Congolese account leaves out its own leaders' failures of governance and their own complicity with the very foreign armies they now blame.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The resource account leaves out that some of the fighting in the Kivus was over land and ethnicity, and had nothing to do with coltan at all.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The peacekeepers' account is written as a story about a mandate too narrow to help. It says less about the missions where its own troops did intervene, and less still about the Congolese government's own failure to protect its citizens.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: And Panzi's account, the one with the least power to change any of it, says almost nothing about the men and boys the record also counts among the survivors, or about Congolese women who fought as combatants rather than only survived as victims.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: M23, backed by Rwanda according to the United Nations Group of Experts, seized Goma, a city of two million people, in November two thousand twelve. It returned in two thousand twenty two.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: As of two thousand twenty six, eastern Congo has over one hundred twenty active armed groups.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The ground underneath them holds an estimated twenty four trillion dollars in minerals. In two thousand twenty three, the average Congolese person's income for the year was six hundred fifty four dollars.
